Where it began

Michael Bevan was born in Belconnen, Canberra, on 8 May 1970, and he became the first Canberra-born cricketer to play for Australia. His first senior club was Weston Creek, he was at the ACT Academy of Sport, and in 1989 he held a scholarship at the Australian Cricket Academy.

He made his first-class debut for South Australia in 1989-90 and scored a hundred in that first match, against Western Australia. After a single season he moved to New South Wales, where he spent most of his career.

The player

His fame came in one-day cricket. He played 232 one-day internationals for Australia and was part of the sides that won the 1999 and 2003 World Cups. On New Year's Day 1996 at the Sydney Cricket Ground, Australia were 6 for 38 chasing 173 against the West Indies; his unbeaten 78 got them home with a boundary off the very last ball. In the 2003 World Cup against England he came together with Andy Bichel at 135 for 8, needing 70 more, and was 74 not out when Australia got there in the last over.

In Tests he played 18 matches between 1994 and 1998, scoring 785 runs at 29.07 with six fifties and a best of 91. His left-arm wrist spin brought 29 wickets at 24.24, including ten in a match against the West Indies at Adelaide. He made 82 on his Test debut, against Pakistan, in 1994.

What made him special

He had a rare gift for staying calm with the game on the line. In 45 successful Australian run chases he finished unbeaten 25 times, which is how he earned the nickname The Finisher, and later the Pyjama Picasso. He worked the ball into gaps rather than over the ropes, hitting just 21 sixes in 232 matches, and across all his List A cricket he made 15,103 runs at an average of 57.86.

The Test runs never flowed quite as freely as the one-day ones, and a Test hundred eluded him. The Sheffield Shield made up for it: for Tasmania in 2004–05 he made 1,464 first-class runs, a record for a season at the time.

Away from the middle

In England he played for four counties, Yorkshire, Leicestershire, Sussex and Kent, and finished runners-up at the 1998 Commonwealth Games, the first to include cricket. After retiring in January 2007 he coached Kings XI Punjab in the IPL and became a speaker. Australia's greatest one-day team, chosen in 2007, included him, in 2025 he joined the Australian Cricket Hall of Fame, and the player of the match in the domestic one-day final receives the Michael Bevan Medal.

And finally

In 2020 he turned up in disguise as Hammerhead on The Masked Singer Australia, and was only the second singer to be sent home. For once, The Finisher did not see things through to the end.
